title: Three intoxications
hook: the pride of youth, of health, of life (AN 3.38)

segments.voice: Yesterday: a lump of salt and a great river, and your line, widen your heart first. Did your heart widen once? Today the Buddha remembers his own childhood, in his own words. Day six hundred sixty-one.

We've heard the palace story told about him: the sheltered prince, the four sights. In this short discourse from the Book of Threes, the Buddha tells it himself, and the details are startlingly specific. I was delicate, monks, he says, most delicate. At my father's home, lotus ponds were made just for me, one of blue lotuses, one of red, one of white. I wore only fine cloth from Kasi. A white sunshade was held over me day and night, so cold and heat, dust and dew wouldn't touch me. Today: three intoxications.
screen: `IN HIS OWN WORDS.` → `THREE LOTUS PONDS, BLUE, RED, WHITE.` → `A WHITE SUNSHADE, DAY AND NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The memory in AN 3.38 keeps going. He had three palaces, one for winter, one for summer, one for the rains. During the rainy months he stayed in the rains palace, entertained by musicians, and didn't come down at all. In other homes, he says, servants were fed broken rice with sour gruel. In his father's house, even the servants ate fine rice and meat. Then the turn. Even with all that, he says, a thought came to me. An untaught person, who is himself subject to aging, sees someone old and feels disgust and shame, forgetting that he will age too. That isn't fitting for me, he thought. And as he reflected, the intoxication of youth left him completely. The same with illness: the untaught are repelled by the sick, though they'll fall ill too. The intoxication of health left him. The same with death. The intoxication of life left him. The Pali word is mada, a word used for drunkenness, for the madness of pride. Youth, health, being alive: none of them are bad. The intoxication is the feeling that they're mine to keep, and that the old, the sick and the dying are some other kind of person. In the very next discourse he names what these three intoxications do. A person drunk on youth, or health, or life, acts badly in body, speech and mind. It's easy to see how: the intoxication whispers that there's plenty of time. Here's what's moving about the discourse. It isn't a lecture on aging. It's a man remembering the white sunshade, and the moment he saw it couldn't keep anything off him forever.
screen: `THREE PALACES, ONE FOR EACH SEASON` · `DISGUST AT THE OLD, FORGETTING ONESELF` · `MADA: DRUNK ON YOUTH, HEALTH, LIFE` · `THE SUNSHADE CAN'T KEEP IT OFF` · then, large: `THE THREE INTOXICATIONS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and feel the body as it is today: the age it is, the health it has, the life that's in it. Let a little gratitude in for each. Then notice, gently, whether any of the three has a grip of pride: I'm too young for that, I never get sick, there's always tomorrow. Choose one, and soften it. Try the plain thought: this too will change. Not with fear. Just with clearer eyes, and kinder ones toward anyone older or sicker than you. The bell holds the time.
Three intoxications. In AN 3.38, the Buddha, remembering his sheltered youth, names the pride of youth, of health, and of life, and tells how each one left him. Today's word.
Your line: the three intoxications. When you see someone older, or ill, today, catch any flinch, and remember: this is my road too. Day six hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers draw on this discourse when speaking about aging, illness and death, and some meditators reflect on all three as a way to loosen the pride of youth, health and life.

myth: in AN 3.38 the Buddha tells of his sheltered youth himself
he describes the lotus ponds, the Kasi cloth, the white sunshade and the three palaces.
the discourse says youth, health and life are bad
the intoxication is the problem: the pride that forgets one will age, sicken and die.
the untaught feel disgust at the old, forgetting they will age too
seeing that, the Buddha says, the intoxication of youth left him.

fork.setup: you're a young prince with three palaces and a white sunshade held over you. you see someone old and feel a flash of disgust. what does AN 3.38 say comes next?
options: see that you're subject to aging too, and let the pride of youth go.
order the old person out of sight.
fork.reveal: the Buddha says he reflected that disgust wasn't fitting for one who will age, and the intoxication of youth left him.

original.note: Pali mada: intoxication, pride; yobbana-mada, arogya-mada, jivita-mada: of youth, health and life.

trapdoor: what you thought: three intoxications means three kinds of drinking.
what it means: in AN 3.38, the pride of youth, health and life, which makes us forget we too will age, sicken and die.

what a scholar hears: here the Buddha describes his palace youth in the first person; in the suttas the four sights are told of the past buddha Vipassi (DN 14), and some scholars think they were applied to Gotama later, in the commentaries and biographies.
recall: as he says, so he does

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 3.38 (Sukhumala Sutta; AN 3.39 in some editions)
Anguttara Nikaya 3.39 (Mada Sutta; AN 3.40 in some editions)

notes: AN 3.38 paraphrased (Bodhi numbers it AN 3.39). Confirm the details: three lotus ponds (blue, red, white), Kasi sandalwood and Kasi cloth, the white parasol held day and night against cold, heat, dust, grass and dew, three palaces for winter, summer and rains, four months in the rains palace with female musicians, servants' food (broken rice with sour gruel elsewhere; rice and meat at his father's).
The hook uses 'I was delicate, most delicate' as paraphrase, not quotation.
The following sutta (Mada) on the three intoxications leading to misconduct of body, speech and mind: confirm numbering.

The trapdoor's note that the four sights are told of Vipassi in DN 14 and later applied to Gotama is a standard scholarly observation; 'one of the few first-person memories' should be checked (others exist, e.g. MN 26, MN 36).

Reviewer: the teach had stated that people drunk on youth, health or life act badly 'because they think there's plenty of time' as if from the Mada Sutta; the reason is now framed as the script's own reading. The trapdoor's claim that the four sights 'was attached to Gotama' is now softened to 'many scholars think'; traditional Buddhists generally hold the four sights to be Gotama's own story, so a Keeper should confirm the framing.

Review (y2 editor pass): the HOW line taught the five recollections, which is day 665's subject; replaced. Cut the invented 'morning' of his realization, the 'one of the rare passages' superlative, and 'many scholars' (now 'some').
